subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 7! In this unit you will learn all about time – how we measure it, name it, and use it to plan our day. Time is passing all around you, every moment. The sun rises and sets, the days of the week follow one another, and the months roll by until a whole year has gone past. When Amina waits for sunset, when Yusuf counts the days until a family celebration, or when Halima checks the calendar to see how many weeks are left until the school holidays, they are all thinking about time.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

outcomes: Name the units of time – second, minute, hour, day, week, month, year – and put them in order from shortest to longest.
Say how the units are related, such as 60 seconds = 1 minute and 7 days = 1 week.
Name the days of the week in order and the months of the year in order.
Read and understand a calendar, and find a date on it.
Write a date in numbers (05/06/2022) and in words (Sunday 5th June 2022).
Work out yesterday, today and tomorrow from any given day.
Estimate how long an activity will take, then measure it and compare.

concepts.title: The Units of Time
concepts.explanation:
We measure time using different units, from very short ones to very long ones. Just as we use centimetres for short lengths and kilometres for long journeys, we use small units of time for quick things and big units for long stretches of time. Let us meet each one.

A second is the shortest unit you will use. It is very quick – about the time it takes to clap your hands once, blink your eyes, or say ‘good morning’. When Farah times a fast race, she counts in seconds.

A minute is longer than a second. In fact, 60 seconds make one minute. A minute is about how long it takes to brush your teeth, tie your shoelaces, or wash your hands properly before eating. It is a handy unit for short activities.

An hour is longer still. 60 minutes make one hour. An hour is about the length of one lesson at school, or the time to watch a long children's programme. From one mealtime to the next is often about an hour or two. There are 24 hours in one day.

A day goes from one morning to the next and includes the whole night while you sleep. 24 hours make one day. Each day has its own name – we will meet the seven day names very soon. There are 7 days in one week.

A week is 7 days long. Many things in life are planned by the week: the school week, the market days, and the weekly rest of the weekend. There are about 4 weeks in one month.

A month is longer than a week. Each month has a name, like January or December. Most months have 30 or 31 days, but February is special with only 28 days (or 29 in a leap year). There are 12 months in one year.
concepts.example: A year is a long unit of time. A year is how long it takes the Earth to travel all the way around the Sun. There are 365 days in a year (366 in a leap year), which is the same as 12 months or about 52 weeks. You celebrate your birthday once every year.

concepts.title: Ordering Units of Time
concepts.explanation:
Notice how each unit is bigger than the one before it. A second fits inside a minute, a minute fits inside an hour, an hour fits inside a day, and so on, all the way up to a year. It is like a set of nesting bowls: the smallest bowl fits inside a slightly bigger one, which fits inside a bigger one still.

Knowing this order helps you answer many questions. If Hassan asks, ‘Which is longer, a week or a day?’ you look at the order and see that week comes after day, so a week is longer. If Khadija asks, ‘Which is shorter, a minute or an hour?’ you see that minute comes before hour, so a minute is shorter. Whenever you are unsure, picture the ordered list in your mind and read it from short to long.
concepts.example: You can practise this order out loud like a little chant: ‘second, minute, hour, day, week, month, year.’ Say it forwards and then backwards until it stays firmly in your memory. Sagal likes to say it while walking to the well, one unit for each step. The more you say it, the more it becomes automatic, and then ordering-time questions become quick and easy.

concepts.title: How the Units Are Related
concepts.explanation:
These relationships let you answer real questions. If Omar knows that 1 minute is 60 seconds, then 2 minutes must be 60 + 60 = 120 seconds. If Zahra knows that 1 week is 7 days, then 2 weeks must be 7 + 7 = 14 days. You simply add the same amount again for each extra unit. This is a first taste of the multiplying you will do in later units – for now, adding the amount again is perfect.

It also works the other way. If Idris has 14 days, he can group them into sevens: 7 days and 7 days make 2 weeks. If Maryam counts 24 months, she groups them into twelves: 12 and 12 make 2 years. Grouping the small units into the big units is a skill you will use again and again.

concepts.title: The Days of the Week
concepts.explanation:
There are 7 days in a week, and each one has its own name. Here they are in order:

The days always follow this order, and then they start again. After Sunday comes Monday once more, round and round, week after week. This is called a cycle – the days repeat in a never-ending ring of seven. If today is Friday, then in exactly seven days it will be Friday again.

Some days have special jobs. Monday to Friday are usually school days and working days, when Nuur Academy is open and the markets are busy. Saturday and Sunday together make the weekend, a time for rest, family and play. Friday is a very special day for many families, the day of the week when the market is busiest and families gather together.
concepts.example: It really helps to learn the day names in order so you can say them without stopping. Ibrahim chants them on the walk to the market: ‘Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday.’ Once you know the order, you can answer questions like ‘What day comes after Wednesday?’ (Thursday) or ‘What day comes before Saturday?’ (Friday) without having to start from Monday each time.

concepts.title: The Months of the Year
concepts.explanation:
There are 12 months in a year, and like the days, each one has a name and a fixed order. Here they are:

January, February, March (the start of the year)

October, November, December (the end of the year)

After December, the year ends and a new year begins again with January. So the months, like the days, go round in a cycle. Learning them in order helps you answer questions such as ‘What month comes after August?’ (September) or ‘What month comes before April?’ (March).

‘Thirty days has September, April, June, and November. All the rest have thirty-one, except February alone, which has twenty-eight days clear, and twenty-nine in each leap year.’
concepts.example: Say this rhyme a few times and it will stick in your memory. The months named in the rhyme – September, April, June and November – are the ones with 30 days. February is the short one. Every other month has 31 days. So if Noor wants to know how many days are in June, the rhyme tells her: June is named, so it has 30 days.

concepts.title: Reading a Calendar
concepts.explanation:
A calendar is a chart that shows the days, weeks and months of a year. It helps us keep track of dates and plan ahead. Every home benefits from a calendar: it shows when the weekend falls, when a birthday is coming, and how many days remain until a family celebration.

A calendar page for one month has these parts:

The name of the month at the top (for example, MARCH).

The days of the week written along the top row (Mo Tu We Th Fr Sa Su).

The dates – the numbers 1 up to 28, 29, 30 or 31 – filling the grid.

Sometimes special marks for holidays, birthdays, or family events.

Here is a calendar for March 2023 to practise on:

To read a calendar, follow these steps. First, find the month you need. Second, look at the day names along the top. Third, find the date (the number) you are looking for. Fourth, follow up the column from that number to read which day of the week it falls on.

Let us use the March calendar. To find the day for March 15th, look down until you find 15, then follow up its column to the top: it is under We, so March 15th is a Wednesday. To find the first Sunday, look down the ‘Su’ column and read the first number: it is 5, so the first Sunday is March 5th. To count how many Tuesdays there are, look down the ‘Tu’ column: 7, 14, 21, 28 – that is 4 Tuesdays.
concepts.example: Calendars have lovely patterns. The same day of the week appears every 7 numbers down a column (7, 14, 21, 28). Once you can read one calendar, you can read any calendar in the world, because they are all built the same way.

methods.title: How to order units of time
methods.example: Put these units in order from shortest to longest: week, second, hour, day, minute.
steps: Picture the full order: second, minute, hour, day, week, month, year.
Pick out only the units you were given.
Keep them in that same order, shortest first.

methods.title: How to write a date in words
methods.example: Match each on the left to its equal on the right: 1 minute, 1 hour, 1 day, 1 week.
steps: Read the day number, then add its ending (st, nd, rd, th).
Name the month from its number (1 = January … 12 = December).
Add the year. Include the day of the week if you know it.

methods.title: How to estimate and measure time
methods.example: Fill in the gaps: Monday, ___, Wednesday, ___, Friday, ___, ___.
steps: Think of a similar activity you have done before.
Make a sensible estimate.
Measure the real time with a clock or stopwatch.
Compare your estimate with the real time.

methods.title: Missing months of the year
methods.example: Which month comes after July, and which month comes before April?
steps: Say the months in order.
After July comes August.
Before April comes March.
Saying the list in order is the surest way to answer.

methods.title: Read a calendar
methods.example: Using the March 2023 calendar above, what day of the week is March 22nd?
steps: Find 22 in the grid, then follow its column up to the day names.
The 22 sits in the ‘We’ column (with 1, 8, 15, 22, 29), so March 22nd is a Wednesday.
Check by counting from the 1st along the same column to make sure you land on 22.

methods.title: Write a date in words
steps: The 30 is the day, 11 is the month (November), and 2022 is the year.
So in words it is 30th November 2022.
Remember the ‘th’ ending on the 30.

workedExamples.title: Order the units of time
workedExamples.prompt: Put these units in order from shortest to longest: week, second, hour, day, minute.
workedExamples.solution: Think of the full order — second, minute, hour, day, week, month, year. Pick out only the ones we were given, keeping that order: second, minute, hour, day, week. The second is shortest and the week is longest.

workedExamples.title: Match the time relationships
workedExamples.prompt: Match each on the left to its equal on the right: 1 minute, 1 hour, 1 day, 1 week.
workedExamples.solution: 1 minute = 60 seconds; 1 hour = 60 minutes; 1 day = 24 hours; 1 week = 7 days. Learn these four facts and many time questions become easy.

workedExamples.title: Missing days of the week
workedExamples.prompt: Fill in the gaps: Monday, ___, Wednesday, ___, Friday, ___, ___.
workedExamples.solution: Say the days in order to find each gap. After Monday comes Tuesday; after Wednesday comes Thursday; after Friday come Saturday and Sunday. The full week is Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday.

workedExamples.title: Missing months of the year
workedExamples.prompt: Which month comes after July, and which month comes before April?
workedExamples.solution: Say the months in order. After July comes August. Before April comes March. Saying the list in order is the surest way to answer.

workedExamples.title: Read a calendar
workedExamples.prompt: Using a March 2023 calendar (the 1st is a Wednesday), what day of the week is March 22nd?
workedExamples.solution: Find 22 in the grid, then follow its column up to the day names. The 22 sits in the ‘We’ column (with 1, 8, 15, 22, 29), so March 22nd is a Wednesday.

workedExamples.title: Write a date in words
workedExamples.solution: The 30 is the day, 11 is the month (November), and 2022 is the year. So in words it is 30th November 2022. Remember the ‘th’ ending on the 30.

workedExamples.title: Write a date in numbers
workedExamples.prompt: Write Saturday 25th December 2021 in numbers as DD/MM/YYYY.
workedExamples.solution: The day is 25, December is the 12th month, and the year is 2021. So we write 25/12/2021. December already has two digits (12), and 25 has two digits, so no extra zeros are needed.

workedExamples.title: Yesterday and tomorrow
workedExamples.prompt: If today is Wednesday, what day was yesterday and what day will tomorrow be?
workedExamples.solution: Step back one day for yesterday: Tuesday. Step forward one day for tomorrow: Thursday. So yesterday was Tuesday and tomorrow will be Thursday.

workedExamples.title: Order by duration
workedExamples.prompt: Put these in order from shortest to longest: sleeping at night, clapping your hands once, eating breakfast, reading a chapter.
workedExamples.solution: Think about how long each takes. Clapping (about 1 second) is shortest, then eating breakfast (a few minutes), then reading a chapter (longer), then sleeping at night (many hours) is longest. The order is: clapping your hands once, eating breakfast, reading a chapter, sleeping at night.

workedExamples.title: Plan within a time
workedExamples.prompt: Yusuf has 1 hour (60 minutes) of free time. He wants to read a book (20 minutes), draw a picture (15 minutes), and do a puzzle (10 minutes). Does it all fit?
workedExamples.solution: Add the times: 20 + 15 + 10 = 45 minutes. Since 45 is less than 60, it all fits, with 60 − 45 = 15 minutes to spare. Good planning leaves a little time over.

activities.title: Make Your Own Calendar
activities.materials: paper, a ruler, a pencil, coloured pencils.
steps: Draw a grid with 7 boxes across (one for each day) and 5 rows down.
Write the day names along the top: Mo Tu We Th Fr Sa Su.
Fill in the dates for this month, starting on the correct day.
Colour the weekends and mark any special days, like a birthday or festival.
Keep your calendar on the wall and cross off each day as it passes.

activities.title: Time a Task (Stopwatch Fun)
activities.materials: a clock, watch, or phone that shows seconds, and a partner.
steps: One person picks a task: counting to 20, saying the alphabet, or standing on one foot.
The other person says ‘GO!’ and starts timing, then stops when the task is finished.
Write down how many seconds it took.
Swap over and try again. Did the time change the second time?
This activity, based on the ‘Time a Task’ project, helps you feel how long a second and a minute really are.

activities.title: Estimate Then Measure (Investigation)
activities.materials: a timer and a list of small tasks.
steps: Before you start, estimate how long each task will take (for example, writing your name, tidying your books, walking to the gate).
Now measure the real time with the timer.
Compare your estimate to the real time. Were you close?
Do it again with new tasks. Do your estimates get better with practice?

activities.title: Days and Months Memory Game
steps: Write each day of the week on a card, and each month of the year on another card.
Shuffle the day cards and race to put them back in the right order.
Do the same with the month cards. Time yourself and try to beat your record.
Ask a family member to remove one card while you close your eyes – can you say which is missing?

activities.title: The Yesterday–Today–Tomorrow Game (Family Game)
steps: One person calls out a day, for example ‘Thursday’.
The next person must quickly say yesterday (Wednesday) and tomorrow (Friday).
If they are right, they call out the next day for someone else.
Play faster and faster to make it exciting.

activities.title: My Daily Timeline
steps: Draw a long line across your paper for one day, from waking up to sleeping.
Mark on your main activities (school, meals, play, bedtime).
Next to each, write about how long it takes – in minutes or hours.
Show your timeline to your family and talk about how you spend your time.

After your activities, talk or write about: Which activity helped you understand time best? Were your estimates close to the real times? What would you like more practice with – the calendar, the units, or estimating? Share your answer with your teacher at your next session.

rules.title: Units of Time Order
rules.text: Shortest to longest: second, minute, hour, day, week, month, year. Each unit is bigger than the one before it.

rules.title: Time Relationships
rules.text: 60 seconds = 1 minute. 60 minutes = 1 hour. 24 hours = 1 day. 7 days = 1 week. 12 months = 1 year. 365 days = 1 year.

rules.title: Calendar Rule
rules.text: To find the day for a date, follow the date's column UP to the day names. The same weekday repeats every 7 dates down a column.

selfAssessment: I can name the units of time – second, minute, hour, day, week, month, year – and put them in order from shortest to longest.
I can say how the units are related, such as 60 seconds = 1 minute and 7 days = 1 week.
I can name the days of the week in order and the months of the year in order.
I can read and understand a calendar, and find a date on it.
I can write a date in numbers (05/06/2022) and in words (Sunday 5th June 2022).
I can work out yesterday, today and tomorrow from any given day.
I can estimate how long an activity will take, then measure it and compare.
